title: Rear poultry parent stock to sexual maturity after brooding

lessons.title: Rearing breeder pullets and cockerels
lessons.html:
Rearing breeder pullets and cockerels

Parent stock (breeders) are the hens and cocks whose fertile eggs go to the hatchery. From the end of brooding until they start laying (sexual maturity), they are reared with great care. A breeder flock that is too fat, too thin or uneven will lay fewer eggs and give fewer chicks.

Why weight control matters

Broiler breeders come from fast-growing meat birds. If they eat as much as they want, they become too fat, lay poorly and have leg and fertility problems. For this reason they are usually feed restricted: they get a measured amount of feed each day, set by the farm manager from the breed guide.

Feeding restricted birds

  • Weigh out the exact amount of feed for each house or pen.
  • Feed must spread fast so all birds get a fair share at the same time. Feeder lines run quickly and there must be enough feeder space.
  • Watch at feeding time. Small, timid birds must be able to eat.
  • Clean out wet or caked feed.
  • Never give extra feed without instructions.

Males and females

Cockerels and pullets are often reared apart, because males grow differently and need their own feed amounts and weights. Follow the farm plan for each sex.

Weighing

  1. Weigh a sample of birds from different parts of each pen at the same time and day each week.
  2. Record each weight.
  3. The supervisor compares the average and uniformity with the target and decides the feed amount for next week.

Accurate weighing is very important, because feed decisions depend on it.

lessons.title: Grading, lighting and bringing birds into lay
lessons.html:
Grading, lighting and bringing birds into lay

Grading

If a flock is uneven, birds may be sorted (graded) into light, medium and heavy groups in separate pens. Each group then gets the feed it needs to reach target. Grade only as your supervisor directs and handle birds gently.

Lighting

During rearing, breeders usually get short, fixed day lengths so they do not mature too early. Light stimulation (increasing light hours) is started by the manager when birds reach the right age and weight.

  • Never change the light programme.
  • In dark-out houses, keep doors and curtains light-tight.
  • Report broken lights and timers.

Health and bio-security

  • Breeders get a long vaccination programme from the vet. Keep vaccines cold and record each one.
  • Breeder farms follow strict bio-security, because disease in parents can pass to many chicks.
  • Shower in and change clothes where required. Use foot baths.
  • Report sick birds and sudden deaths at once.

Moving to the laying house

  1. Prepare the laying house with nests, feeders, drinkers and slats.
  2. Move birds at the planned age, in dim light, handling gently.
  3. Males are mixed with females at the ratio and time the manager sets.
  4. Make sure birds find water and feed quickly.
  5. Record numbers moved and deaths.

Under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 animals must not be handled cruelly. Never throw birds, carry them by the neck or one wing, or overfill crates.

Key points

  • Breeders are feed restricted to stop them getting too fat.
  • Weigh feed and birds accurately; feed decisions depend on it.
  • Feed must spread fast so all birds eat at once.
  • Light stimulation is decided by the manager, never by workers.
  • Strict bio-security protects the chicks that come from the flock.

options.text: To stop them becoming too fat

quiz.question: Why must feed spread fast to all feeders for breeders?

options.text: Sorting birds into light, medium and heavy groups
